title: Software Evaluation Checklist: A Practical Buyer’s Guide
description: A step-by-step checklist for defining requirements, running comparable product pilots, estimating total cost, checking security and portability, and documenting a defensible software decision.

sections.title: Define the problem before comparing products
sections.body: Start with the work that needs to improve, not with a vendor feature list. Document the current workflow, who performs each step, where delays or errors occur, what data is involved, and what a successful outcome would look like. Ask daily users and process owners to contribute. Separate mandatory requirements from preferences, and write down what evidence would show that a requirement is met. If the current process can be improved through configuration or training, include that option rather than assuming a new purchase is necessary.

sections.title: Build a scoring matrix that can be explained
sections.body: Use weights only after stakeholders agree on what matters. The percentages below are an example structure, not an industry benchmark; change them to match the risk and purpose of your purchase.
rows: Run representative tasks and record pass/fail results, workarounds, and missing capabilities.
Review current vendor documentation, required access controls, retention terms, and contractual commitments.
Test the exact connectors and export/import behavior needed by your stack.
Ask intended users to complete common tasks and record friction without coaching.
Calculate license, usage, add-ons, setup, training, administration, migration, and exit costs.
Verify support channels and contractual service commitments relevant to the chosen plan.

sections.title: Write test cases before vendor demos
sections.body: Prepare a short scenario script using representative data and realistic edge cases. Ask each vendor or pilot account to demonstrate the same workflow: create or import a record, apply the permissions you need, search for it, change its status, trigger a notification or automation, build a report, and export the result. Record what was demonstrated, what was only promised, what required a higher plan, and what could not be tested. A polished demo is not evidence that the product fits your workflow.

sections.title: Run a controlled pilot
sections.body: Keep the pilot small enough to manage but representative enough to reveal problems.
items: Choose a fixed set of tasks and define acceptance criteria before testing.
Use the same inputs and user roles across all candidate products.
Include normal cases, exceptions, permission boundaries, and data-export tests.
Record completion time, errors, workarounds, support requests, and user feedback.
Confirm which features are included in the actual plan being evaluated.
Document any vendor statement that still needs written confirmation.
Do not move sensitive or production data into a trial until its data terms are approved.

sections.title: Calculate total cost of ownership
sections.body: Compare the same period and scope for each candidate. Include seats, usage or storage, required add-ons, onboarding, configuration, integration work, training, administration, support, taxes, renewal terms, and migration or exit costs. For usage-based products, estimate both normal and peak demand and include overages. Keep list prices separate from a quote and record the country, currency, billing term, and date checked. Avoid presenting hypothetical productivity savings as guaranteed ROI; measure the baseline and pilot outcome first.

sections.title: Review security, privacy, and contractual fit
sections.body: Use the vendor's current security and privacy documents and your organization's requirements. Check identity and access management, role permissions, audit events, retention and deletion, data processing, data residency if required, incident response, backups, and export. Confirm whether the required controls apply to the plan and contract you are considering. Do not infer a certification, legal compliance, or uptime guarantee from a marketing page; obtain the applicable evidence and written terms.

sections.title: Plan migration and exit before committing
sections.body: Export a representative sample and test it outside the source product. Check records, relationships, formulas, attachments, comments, permissions, history, and internal links. Identify what needs manual rebuilding, who owns the migration, and how users will be trained. Confirm how data can be exported and deleted at contract end, and whether any proprietary workflow or integration would make switching unusually expensive. Keep a rollback plan until the new workflow is stable.

sections.title: Make the decision and record the evidence
sections.body: Summarize which mandatory requirements passed, which failed, which remain unknown, and what the unknowns would cost or risk. Show the total cost assumptions and the trade-offs behind the recommendation. Document the selected plan, contract terms, owners, implementation dependencies, and review date. A defensible decision is not necessarily the product with the highest total score; a single critical security, migration, or workflow failure can outweigh advantages elsewhere.

sections.title: Post-launch review
sections.body: After rollout, compare actual adoption, operating effort, support needs, usage, and invoices with the pilot assumptions. Ask users where workarounds persist and track whether the original problem improved. Revisit the decision if costs, requirements, product terms, or risk change. This review makes the evaluation reusable for future renewals and prevents an initial purchase from becoming an unchecked long-term commitment.

author: Sarah Chen
